stem: Look! The children ___ in the river.
explanation: "Look!" shows that the action is happening right now, so you need the present progressive: am/is/are + -ing. The simple present (swim) is for habits and facts, not for something you can see at this moment.
hint: Is this happening at the moment or every day?

stem: My grandma ___ to church every Sunday.
explanation: "Every Sunday" is a signal word for a habit, so you need the simple present. With he, she or it the verb gets an -s: she goes. "Go" forgets the -s, and "is going" would mean only right now.
hint: Does she do this once or regularly? And don't forget he/she/it.

stem: Put the verb in the correct tense.

payload.text: Thandi [[0]] (live) in Cape Town since 2019.

explanation: "Since 2019" means the action started in the past and is still going on. For this you need the present perfect (has lived) or the present perfect progressive (has been living). In German you say "wohnt seit", but in English the simple present is wrong here.
hint: Look at the signal word before the year: did it start in the past and continue until now?

stem: We ___ Johannesburg two years ago.
explanation: "Ago" points to a finished time in the past, so you need the simple past. The present perfect (have visited) can never be used with "ago", even though German says "Wir haben ... besucht".
hint: Which tense do you use with a finished time in the past?

stem: Choose the correct word.

payload.text: I have known Sipho [[0]] ten years.

explanation: Use "for" with a period of time (ten years, three weeks) and "since" with a point in time (2019, last summer). "Ten years" is a period, so it must be "for". "Ago" goes with the simple past only.
hint: Is "ten years" a point in time or a length of time?

stem: Choose the correct word.

payload.text: She has been learning Zulu [[0]] last summer.

explanation: "Last summer" is a point in time when the action started, so you need "since". "For" is used with a period of time, for example "for two months".
hint: Does "last summer" tell you when it started or how long it lasted?

stem: Oh, now I ___ what you mean!
explanation: "Understand" is a stative verb: it describes a state of mind, not an action. Stative verbs like understand, know, believe and like are normally not used in the progressive form. "Understands" is wrong because the subject is I.
hint: Is "understand" an action you can watch, or a state?

stem: Put the verbs in the correct tense.

payload.text: While we [[0]] (drive) through Kruger National Park, an elephant suddenly [[1]] (step) onto the road.

explanation: The longer background action (we were driving) is in the past progressive. The short action that interrupts it (an elephant stepped onto the road) is in the simple past. "While" and "suddenly" are typical signal words for this pattern.
hint: Which action was already going on, and which one happened suddenly?

stem: I ___ a real lion yet, but I hope to see one on our safari.
explanation: "Yet" is a signal word for the present perfect: have/has + past participle. The past participle of see is "seen", not "saw" (saw is the simple past form). The simple past "didn't see" does not go with "yet".
hint: Which tense goes with "yet", and what is the third form of see?

stem: Choose the correct verb forms.

payload.text: My brother [[0]] a volunteer job in a township last March. He [[1]] there ever since.

explanation: "Last March" is a finished point in time, so the first verb is simple past (started). "Ever since" means from then until now, so the second verb is present perfect (has worked). The present perfect cannot go with "last March".
hint: Look at the time phrase in each sentence: finished past or until now?

stem: By the time we arrived at the stadium, the match ___.
explanation: Two actions in the past: the match started first, then we arrived. For the earlier action you use the past perfect (had + past participle). "By the time" is a typical signal word. The present perfect does not fit because the whole story is in the past.
hint: Which happened first: the start of the match or our arrival?

stem: Put the verb in the correct tense.

payload.text: When I arrived at the party, Lerato [[0]] (go) home already. I didn't see her at all.

explanation: Lerato left before I arrived, so her action happened earlier in the past. This needs the past perfect: had gone. With the simple past (went) the sentence would mean that she left at the moment you arrived.
hint: She was not there any more when I came. Which tense shows the earlier past action?

stem: Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.
explanation: When you can see now that something is about to happen, you use "going to". The dark clouds are the evidence. "Will" is used for spontaneous decisions and general predictions without clear evidence.
hint: Can you already see a sign that it will happen?

stem: I can't come to your party on Saturday. I ___ my cousins in Pretoria – we bought the train tickets last week.
explanation: The visit is a fixed arrangement: the tickets are already bought. For arranged plans in the future you use the present progressive. "Will visit" sounds like a decision made just now, and the simple present is only used for timetables.
hint: Is this a spontaneous idea or something that is already arranged?

stem: Choose the correct verb form.

payload.text:
A: The phone is ringing!
B: OK, I [[0]] it.

explanation: B decides at the moment of speaking, so this is a spontaneous decision. For spontaneous decisions and offers you use "will". "Going to" is for plans you made before.
hint: Did B plan this before, or decide just now?

stem: Put the verbs in the correct tense.

payload.text: I promise I [[0]] (call) you as soon as I [[1]] (land) in Cape Town.

explanation: A promise is expressed with "will": I will call you. After time words like "as soon as", "when" and "after" you use the simple present, even if you mean the future. So it is "as soon as I land", not "as soon as I will land".
hint: One part is a promise, the other is a time clause with "as soon as".

stem: Which signal word goes with the **simple past**?
explanation: "Yesterday" names a finished time in the past, so it goes with the simple past. "Since", "already" and "so far" connect the past with the present and go with the present perfect.
hint: Which word names a finished time?

stem: Match the signal words with the tense they usually go with.
explanation: "Ago" points to a finished past time, so it takes the simple past. "At the moment" shows an action happening now (present progressive). "Since" connects past and present (present perfect), and "usually" describes a habit (simple present).
hint: Ask yourself: finished past, right now, until now, or a habit?

stem: Which sentences are correct? Choose all correct answers.

options: I have seen Mandela's prison cell on Robben Island last year.
I saw Mandela's prison cell on Robben Island last year.
I have never been to Robben Island.
I have been to Robben Island in 2023.
Have you ever visited Robben Island?

explanation: With a finished time like "last year" or "in 2023" you must use the simple past, so sentences 1 and 4 are wrong. "Never" and "ever" talk about experiences up to now without a fixed time, so they go with the present perfect.
hint: Check each sentence: is a finished time mentioned?

stem: Put the verb in the correct tense.

payload.text: My hands are dirty because I [[0]] (work) in the garden all morning.

explanation: The activity lasted a long time and you can still see the result now (dirty hands). For this you use the present perfect progressive: have been + -ing. "All morning" stresses the duration.
hint: The activity went on for a long time, and you can see its result now.

stem:
A: How long ___ English?
B: For six years – and I still have lessons twice a week.
explanation: The learning started in the past and is still going on, so you need the present perfect progressive. Germans often say "Wie lange lernst du schon?" and use the present tense, but in English that is wrong. "Did you learn" would mean it is finished.
hint: B is still learning. Which tense connects the past with now?

stem: Choose the correct verb forms.

payload.text: Nelson Mandela [[0]] in prison for 27 years. When he [[1]] in 1990, he [[2]] a symbol of hope for millions of people.

explanation: The prison time is finished history, so it is simple past (was). Mandela did not release himself, so you need the passive in the simple past: was released. He became a symbol before 1990, so the earlier action is in the past perfect: had already become.
hint: Think about three things: finished past, who did the releasing, and what happened earlier.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.

options: She has been working at the lodge for three years.
She has been working at the lodge since three years.
She is working at the lodge for three years.
She works at the lodge since three years.

explanation: An action that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect (progressive), not the present tense. "Three years" is a period of time, so you need "for". "Since three years" is a typical mistake from German "seit drei Jahren".
hint: Two things to check: the tense and the word before "three years".

stem: Put the verbs in the correct tense.

payload.text: Ayanda [[0]] (not / see) her grandfather for a long time, so she [[1]] (be) really happy when he visited last weekend.

explanation: The long time without seeing him came before the visit last weekend, so it is in the past perfect: hadn't seen. Her happiness belongs to the visit itself, which is simple past: was. The past perfect always shows the earlier of two past actions.
hint: What came first: the long time apart or the visit?

stem: When you called me at 8 o'clock last night, I ___ a film about the Soweto uprising, so I didn't answer.
explanation: The film was already running when the call came, so it is a background action in the past: past progressive (was watching). "Watched" would mean you started the film after the call. The present tenses do not fit "last night".
hint: Was the film already running when the phone rang?

stem: Choose the correct verb form.

payload.text: Water [[0]] at 100 degrees Celsius.

explanation: This is a scientific fact that is always true, so you use the simple present. "Water" is singular (it), so the verb gets an -s: boils.
hint: Is this true only now or always?

stem: This bag ___ to my sister.
explanation: "Belong" is a stative verb that describes possession, so it is not used in the progressive form. "This bag" is singular, so the verb needs an -s: belongs.
hint: Is belonging an action or a state?

stem: Put the verb in the correct tense.

payload.text: Look, Zanele [[0]] (wear) the new dress she bought yesterday.

explanation: "Look" shows that you can see it at this moment, so you use the present progressive: is wearing. The simple present "wears" would mean she wears it regularly.
hint: Can you see it right now?

stem: Which sentence describes a plan that was decided **before** the moment of speaking?

options: I'm going to study law after school.
Oh, it's cold in here – I'll close the window.
Maybe it will snow in Johannesburg tomorrow.
I think South Africa will win the match.

explanation: "Going to" is used for intentions and plans you made earlier. "I'll close the window" is a spontaneous decision, and the other two sentences are predictions with "will".
hint: Which form do you use for plans and intentions?

stem: Put the verbs in the correct tense.

payload.text: Since the end of apartheid, South Africa [[0]] (change) a lot, but many people still [[1]] (live) in poverty today.

explanation: "Since the end of apartheid" connects the past with the present, so the first verb is present perfect: has changed. The second part describes a general situation today, so you use the simple present: live.
hint: The first part goes from the past until now, the second part describes today.

stem: English ___ in many countries all over the world.
explanation: Nobody in particular is doing the action, so you use the passive: form of be + past participle. In the simple present it is am/is/are + past participle: is spoken. "English speaks" would mean that the language itself is talking.
hint: Does English do the speaking, or is something done to it?

stem: The Harry Potter books ___ by J. K. Rowling.
explanation: The books did not write anything, they were written by someone, so you need the passive. For a finished action in the past it is was/were + past participle: were written. "Wrote" is active and would mean that the books wrote something.
hint: Think about who did the writing: the books or the author?

stem: Put the verb in the passive (simple present).

payload.text: Every year, thousands of trees [[0]] (plant) in our region.

explanation: "Every year" shows a regular action, so you use the simple present passive: am/is/are + past participle. "Trees" is plural, so it is "are planted". Who plants them is not important here.
hint: You need a form of "be" plus the past participle. Is "trees" singular or plural?

stem: Put the verb in the passive (simple past).

payload.text: The new sports hall [[0]] (open) last month.

explanation: "Last month" is a finished time in the past, so you use the simple past passive: was/were + past participle. "The sports hall" is singular, so it is "was opened".
hint: Which signal word shows the tense, and which form of "be" goes with one sports hall?

stem: Our classroom ___ right now, so we have our lessons in the library.
explanation: The action is happening at this moment ("right now") and the classroom is not doing the painting itself. For the present progressive passive you use am/is/are + being + past participle: is being painted. "Is painting" is active and means the classroom paints something.
hint: Is the classroom doing something, or is something happening to it at the moment?

stem: Choose the correct verb form.

payload.text: We are still waiting for our marks. The results of the test [[0]] yet.

explanation: "Yet" is a signal word for the present perfect, and the results are published by someone else, so you need the passive. Present perfect passive: have/has + been + past participle. "Weren't published" is simple past and does not go with "yet".

stem: Put the verb in the passive (simple past).

payload.text: The football match [[0]] (cancel) because of the storm yesterday.

explanation: "Yesterday" shows the simple past, and the match did not cancel anything itself, so it is simple past passive: was + past participle. In British English the past participle is "cancelled" with double l, in American English "canceled".
hint: Which tense does "yesterday" need, and how do you build the passive in that tense?

stem: Active: *Somebody stole my bike last night.* Which passive sentence is correct?

options: My bike was stolen last night.
My bike was stole last night.
My bike is stolen last night.
My bike has been stolen last night.

explanation: The active sentence is simple past, so the passive is simple past too: was + past participle. The past participle of steal is "stolen", not "stole". "Has been stolen" is present perfect, which cannot be used with "last night".
hint: Keep the tense of the active sentence. What is the third form of "steal"?

stem: The new school rules ___ next Monday.
explanation: The rules do not introduce anything themselves, so you need the passive. Future passive: will + be + past participle. Both "be" and the past participle (introduced) are needed.
hint: The future passive has three parts. Which ones are missing in the wrong options?

stem: Put the words in brackets into the passive.

payload.text: Mobile phones [[0]] (must / switch off) during the exam.

explanation: After a modal verb like must, can or should, the passive is: modal + be + past participle. So it is "must be switched off". The phones are switched off by the students, they do not switch off anything themselves.
hint: What always follows a modal verb when you make a passive sentence?

stem: Which sentences are correct? Choose all correct answers.

options: The windows are cleaned every week.
The film was direct by a young woman.
The problem can be solved easily.

explanation: A passive sentence always needs a form of "be" and the past participle (third form). In "was direct" and "has been repair" the -ed ending of the past participle is missing: directed, repaired. The other three sentences use be + past participle correctly.
hint: Check the last verb in each sentence: is it really the third form?

stem:
Why is the passive used in this sentence?

*My phone was stolen at the station.*

options: We don't know or it isn't important who did it.
The action is happening right now.
The sentence talks about the future.
The thief is the most important information.

explanation: The passive is used when the person who does the action is unknown or not important. Here you don't know who stole the phone, so the focus is on the phone. If the thief were the most important information, you would use an active sentence.
hint: Does the sentence tell you who took the phone?

stem: Choose the correct word.

explanation: In a passive sentence you name the person or company that does the action with "by" (by-agent). "From" is a typical mistake from German "von". You only add the by-agent if the information is important.
hint: Which little word introduces the doer in a passive sentence?

stem: Change the active sentence into the passive. Keep the tense.

payload.text: *They have repaired the lift.* → The lift [[0]] (repair).

explanation: The active sentence is in the present perfect (have repaired). The present perfect passive is has/have + been + past participle. "The lift" is singular, so it is "has been repaired".
hint: Find the tense in the active sentence first. Then add "been".

stem: When I got to school, the doors ___ already.
explanation: The doors were locked before I arrived, so you need the past perfect. The doors did not lock anything themselves, so it is past perfect passive: had + been + past participle. "Had locked" is active and would mean that the doors locked something.
hint: Which action happened first, and is it active or passive?

stem: You ___ wear a helmet when you ride a motorbike. It's the law.
explanation: "It's the law" shows that it is necessary, so you use "must" (or "have to"). "Mustn't" means that something is forbidden, and "needn't" means that it is not necessary.
hint: Is wearing a helmet necessary, forbidden or just possible?

stem: You ___ use your phone during the test. It isn't allowed.
explanation: Something that is not allowed is expressed with "mustn't" (must not). "Don't have to" and "needn't" only mean that something is not necessary, you could still do it if you wanted to.
hint: Is using the phone forbidden or only not necessary?

stem: It's Saturday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early.
explanation: There is no school, so getting up early is not necessary. "Not necessary" is "don't have to" or "needn't". "Mustn't" is a typical mistake from German "muss nicht": it means "darf nicht". "Haven't to" does not exist.
hint: Is getting up early forbidden or just not necessary?

stem: Choose the correct modal verb.

payload.text: You look really tired. You [[0]] go to bed earlier.

explanation: To give advice you use "should" (sollte). The speaker thinks going to bed earlier is a good idea. "Shouldn't" and "mustn't" would advise against it, and "needn't" says it isn't necessary.
hint: Is the speaker giving advice for or against going to bed earlier?

explanation: "Must" has no past form. For the past you use "had to". "Yesterday" shows that the sentence is in the past.
hint: "Must" has no past form. Which form of "have to" do you need for yesterday?

stem: When I was five, I ___ swim, but now I'm a good swimmer.
explanation: The sentence talks about the past ("when I was five") and about ability. The past of "can" is "could", so "couldn't" means "konnte nicht". "Can't" is present tense, and "mustn't" and "needn't" are not about ability.
hint: Is the sentence about the past or the present, and is it about ability or rules?

stem: Complete the sentence with the correct form of **be able to**.

hint: "Can" has no future form. How do you build the future with "be able to"?

stem: You ask your teacher for permission: "Excuse me, Mr Brown. ___ I leave the room for a moment, please?"
explanation: To ask for permission you use "may" or "can". "May" is very polite and fits well when you talk to a teacher. "Must I ...?" asks if something is necessary, and "Should I ...?" asks for advice.
hint: Are you asking for permission, advice or whether something is necessary?

stem: Match the modal verbs with their meaning.

pairs: It is possible, or you are able to do it.

explanation: "Must" shows that something is necessary, "mustn't" that it is forbidden. "Needn't" means it is not necessary, but allowed. "Can" is about ability or possibility, and "should" gives advice.
hint: Start with the pair that is easiest for you and then think about must and mustn't.

stem: How do you say *"Du musst nicht mitkommen."* in English?
explanation: "Nicht müssen" means that something is not necessary, so it is "don't have to" or "needn't". "Mustn't" and "must not" are the same and mean "nicht dürfen". "Haven't to" is not correct English.
hint: Does the German sentence mean "not necessary" or "not allowed"?

stem: Choose the correct words.

stem: Which sentences are correct? Choose all correct answers.

options: We will have to leave early.

explanation: Modal verbs never get an -s in the third person (she can, he must). Two modal verbs can't stand together, so "will can" is wrong: you say "will be able to". "Will have to" is correct because "have to" is not a modal verb.
hint: Look for an -s after a modal verb and for two modal verbs next to each other.

stem: Look at the sign: *No swimming.* You ___ swim here.
explanation: The sign forbids swimming, so you use "mustn't". "Don't have to" and "needn't" would mean that swimming is not necessary but still allowed. "Can" would mean it is allowed.
hint: Does the sign say that swimming is forbidden or just not necessary?

stem: Which sentence means the same as: *It isn't necessary to bring your own lunch.*
